separable: separable — *key up the team*, and *key them up*; with a pronoun it must split: *key him up*, never ✗ *key up him*. Most often passive: *he was keyed up*.
gloss: To make someone tense and over-excited before something important.
examples: She was so *keyed up* before the interview that she couldn't eat.
The coach's speech *keyed* the whole team *up* for the second half.
Too much coffee *keys* him *up* and ruins his sleep.

separable: separable — *kick up dust*, and *kick it up*; with a pronoun it must split: *kick it up*, never ✗ *kick up it*.
gloss: To send dust, dirt, or spray flying into the air.
examples: The truck *kicked up* a cloud of dust on the gravel road.
The dust settles for a minute, and then another car *kicks* it *up* again.
The horses were *kicking up* mud all over the track.

separable: inseparable in this sense — the object is a set noun that never moves: *kick up a fuss*, never ✗ *kick a fuss up*.
gloss: To make a loud, angry fuss about something.
examples: Parents *kicked up* a fuss when the school cut the music program.
If you *kick up* a stink about the bill, they usually waive it.
The neighbors have been *kicking up* a racket since midnight.
contrast: Almost always followed by a fixed noun — *a fuss*, *a stink*, *a racket*, *a row*. Learners who say ✗ *kick up an anger* have taken it for a free pattern; it isn't one.

ru: отстранять, отстранить от дел (повысив в должности)
separable: separable — the person goes in the middle: *kick him upstairs*, *kick the manager upstairs*.
gloss: To move someone into a job with a grander title but less real power.
examples: When they couldn't fire him, they *kicked* him *upstairs*.
She was *kicked upstairs* to vice president of special projects.
The board is *kicking* the old guard *upstairs* one by one.

separable: separable — *kiss off the whole staff*, and *kiss them off*; with a pronoun it must split: *kiss him off*, never ✗ *kiss off him*.
gloss: To get rid of someone abruptly and rudely.
examples: Management decided to *kiss off* the entire night shift.
She *kissed* him *off* with a two-line text.
He's been *kissing off* his old friends ever since the promotion.

ru: опрокидывать, опрокинуть (рюмку); выпивать залпом, выпить залпом
separable: separable — *knock back a shot*, and *knock it back*; with a pronoun it must split: *knock it back*, never ✗ *knock back it*.
gloss: To drink something, usually alcohol, quickly and in one go.
examples: He *knocks back* a beer the minute he gets home.
She poured the whiskey and *knocked* it *back* in one swallow.
They were *knocking back* margaritas all afternoon.

separable: separable — *knock up his girlfriend*, and *knock her up*; with a pronoun it must split: *knock her up*, never ✗ *knock up her*.
gloss: To make a woman pregnant — crude slang, and offensive in most company.
examples: He *knocked up* his girlfriend their senior year.
Everyone assumed someone had *knocked* her *up*.
Back then, *knocking* a girl *up* meant you got married.
contrast: A transatlantic trap. In American English this is the only common meaning, and it is vulgar. In British English *knock up* can mean to wake someone by knocking or to make something quickly (*knock up a meal*) — say that to an American and you will be misheard.

separable: inseparable — nothing comes between; the pressure follows *to*: *knuckle under to the board*.
gloss: To stop resisting and give in to pressure or authority.
examples: The union refused to *knuckle under* to the new contract terms.
After six weeks on strike, management finally *knuckled under*.
He's not *knuckling under* without a fight.

separable: inseparable — the target always follows *into*: *lace into him*, never ✗ *lace him into*.
gloss: To attack someone fiercely, usually with angry words.
examples: His father *laced into* him for wrecking the car.
She *laces into* anyone who shows up unprepared.
The senator kept *lacing into* the press all afternoon.

separable: separable — *lace up your boots*, and *lace them up*; with a pronoun it must split: *lace them up*, never ✗ *lace up them*.
transitivity: both — transitive (*lace up your skates*), intransitive (*lace up and get on the ice*)
gloss: To fasten shoes or boots by pulling the laces tight and tying them.
examples: *Lace up* your boots — the trail is all mud today.
He *laced* his skates *up* and stepped onto the ice.
She's been *lacing up* every morning since she started training.

separable: inseparable — nothing splits it; what is gripped follows *to*: *latch on to the railing*.
gloss: To take hold of something and stay firmly attached to it.
examples: The baby wouldn't *latch on* for the first two days.
A burr *latched on* to my sock and rode all the way home.
Once an idea *latches on*, he won't let it go.
contrast: Bare *latch on* is intransitive — it describes the gripping itself. Written as one word with an object, *latch onto*, it means to seize on an idea or attach yourself to a person: *he latched onto the new boss*.

separable: separable — *liquor up the groomsmen*, and *liquor them up*; very common in the passive, *get liquored up*.
transitivity: both — transitive (*they liquored him up*), intransitive (*we liquored up before the show*)
gloss: To get drunk, or to get someone else drunk.
examples: They all got *liquored up* before the tailgate.
His buddies *liquored* him *up* and put him on the wrong flight.
Nobody's *liquoring up* on a Tuesday night.

separable: always split, and the object is always *it*: *live it up*, never ✗ *live up it* and never with any other object.
gloss: To enjoy yourself in an extravagant, carefree way.
examples: They *lived* it *up* in Vegas for four days straight.
He's *living* it *up* on his severance check.
You only turn thirty once, so *live* it *up*.
contrast: Do not confuse it with *live up to*, which means to meet a standard: *the movie lived up to the hype*. Same base verb, completely different sentence.

ru: заботиться, позаботиться (о ком-л.); присматривать, присмотреть (за кем-л.)
separable: inseparable — the object always follows *after*: *look after the kids*, *look after them*, never ✗ *look them after*.
gloss: To take care of someone or something.
examples: Could you *look after* the dog while we're away?
She *looked after* her grandmother for three years.
Who's *looking after* the store this weekend?
contrast: Three *look* phrases that learners mix up: *look after* = take care of, *look for* = try to find, *look into* = investigate. *I'm looking after the baby* and *I'm looking for the baby* are very different situations.

separable: inseparable — the person follows *on*: *look down on him*, never ✗ *look him down on*.
gloss: To regard someone as inferior and not worth respect.
examples: He *looks down on* anyone who didn't go to college.
They *looked down on* her accent for years.
I'm tired of being *looked down on* for where I grew up.
contrast: The opposite is *look up to* (admire): *she looks up to her older sister*. Keep the particles straight — *look down on* is contempt, *look up to* is respect.

ru: входить, войти (в семью, в круг — через брак)
separable: inseparable — the family or the money follows *into*: *marry into a fortune*.
gloss: To become part of a family, class, or fortune by marrying someone who already belongs to it.
examples: She *married into* one of the oldest families in the state.
Having *married into* a farming family, he learned to drive a tractor at forty.
You don't just *marry into* that kind of money.

separable: separable — *marry off their daughters*, and *marry them off*; with a pronoun it must split: *marry her off*, never ✗ *marry off her*.
gloss: To arrange a marriage for someone, usually your own child.
examples: Her parents *married* her *off* at eighteen.
The family was determined to *marry off* all four daughters.
He's *marrying* his niece *off* to a business partner.

separable: separable — *pass off bad checks*, and *pass them off*; with a pronoun it must split: *pass it off*, never ✗ *pass off it*.
gloss: To get rid of something fake or worthless by giving it to someone who takes it as genuine.
examples: He *passed off* counterfeit twenties at three different stores.
The dealer *passes* his worst cars *off* on first-time buyers.
Somebody's been *passing off* bad checks all over town.
